name: Morvacet
description: Morvacet is a targeted amygdala-limbic inhibitor designed to chemically suppress acute grief responses without impairing cognitive function or motor control. It selectively dampens the neural pathways associated with loss-processing, allowing users to maintain productivity during bereavement periods. Originally developed for emergency trauma workers, it became Novafold's best-selling product after the 2187 Lakewall Collapse left tens of thousands grieving and unable to work.
effects: Suppression of acute grief and mourning responses
Reduction in crying reflex and somatic grief symptoms
Maintained cognitive clarity and work performance
Mild emotional distance from recent events
side_effects: Delayed mourning syndrome — grief stored rather than processed
Emotional blunting that extends beyond grief to joy and intimacy
Long-term use linked to complicated grief disorder
Dependency driven by fear of confronting suppressed loss
Rare: complete dissociation from the lost relationship — users may lose the ability to feel the loss at all
cultural_context: In GLMZ's relentless productivity culture, grief is treated as a scheduling problem. Employers in Tier 2-3 routinely suggest — sometimes mandate — Morvacet use for employees returning after loss. The drug has become culturally synonymous with the city's brutal pragmatism: you take it, you go back to work, and you deal with the grief later — except 'later' never comes. On the Shelf, it's called 'the Blanket' and is used recreationally as a general emotional numbing agent. Grief counselors and mental health advocates have lobbied to have it reclassified as restricted for years, without success.
story_hooks: A Tier 2 dock worker has been on Morvacet for two years since losing his daughter — his employer keeps renewing his prescription because his performance metrics are excellent. A street doc recognizes the signs of severe delayed mourning syndrome and must decide whether to intervene.

A Novafold whistleblower has internal studies showing Morvacet causes permanent grief-processing impairment with extended use — studies that were buried before the drug's approval. The data is worth money to journalists, rival corps, and regulators.
Someone is using Morvacet to suppress guilt, not grief — and the drug is working just well enough that they're about to do something irreversible.
